doc.title: Hubert Laws — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Contemporary composers, Stravinsky and Boulez at the Philharmonic
summary: Laws is not familiar with Messiaen or Ligeti, loves Stravinsky, and did not like Bartok. He recalls Pierre Boulez conducting modern music and Julius Baker's dislike of it.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: How about contemporary composers, or at least from the mid- to late twentieth century, like Messiaen or Ligiti or any of those?

No. I don’t know. I’m not too familiar with them, I should say. I’m not going to put down the compositions. I don’t – but Igor Stravinsky. Here again, he’s Russian. Stravinsky. I love his Firebird and his Rite of Spring.
We know about Rite of Spring.
I haven’t heard anything that really impressed me about Bartok.
Miraculous Mandarin, no? How about his string quartets?

Nope. No, it didn’t move me. I remember a time sitting – when I played with the Philharmonic, Pierre Boulez was conducting also. He succeeded – I think he came after [Leonard] Bernstein. Played with Bernstein, Boulez, and then came Zubin Mehta. We used to play – Boulez loved modern music. He was crazy about that stuff. I remember we played a concert down in the Village. We were going to try to appeal to the in crowd, I guess you’d call them. I remember Julius Baker. He – we played that music. When the conductor wasn’t looking, he’d do this. That’s the way he felt about the music. He felt like it stunk. It has to have some appeal to me, to my spirit, for me to really appreciate it and like it and want to hear it again. That’s what I find myself doing when I’m listening to these Russian composers I mentioned.
